requirements.requirement: Only root and opsadmin can schedule cron jobs on node1
requirements.summary: /etc/cron.allow was created containing exactly 'root' and 'opsadmin' with correct ownership (root:root, 644). A test user (crontestdeny) not listed was directly verified to be blocked from both crontab -l and crontab install with 'not allowed to use this program (crontab)'. Both root and opsadmin were directly verified able to install, list, and remove crontabs. The restriction and its enforcement were re-verified post-reboot with a second unauthorized test user (crontestdeny2), also blocked.

requirements.requirement: opsadmin account exists and is usable for cron scheduling
requirements.summary: opsadmin did not exist at baseline; executor created it via useradd -m, then confirmed it could schedule and list cron jobs both before and after the restart.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol: pre-restart healthy baseline, restart acknowledgement, changed boot identity, and recovered service/config/access-control state
requirements.summary: Pre-restart baseline captured boot_id 15443601-..., crond active, cron.allow contents, and opsadmin identity. A backgrounded systemctl reboot was scheduled and acknowledged. The node was briefly unreachable (connection timeout), then returned with a new boot_id (3b4c4dd3-...) confirming an actual reboot, matching the fixed after_executor boot-identity snapshot. Post-restart, crond was active, /etc/cron.allow persisted with root/opsadmin, opsadmin could schedule/list a cron job, and a fresh unauthorized test user was blocked, directly demonstrating a full pre-disruption/disruption/recovery transition.

overall_summary: The executor correctly restricted cron scheduling on node1 to root and opsadmin via /etc/cron.allow, with direct before/after evidence that unauthorized users are blocked and root/opsadmin retain access. The independent node-restart evidence protocol was also satisfied end-to-end: healthy pre-restart baseline, restart acknowledgement, a changed boot identity confirming an actual reboot, and full recovery of crond, cron.allow contents, and access-control enforcement afterward. Test artifacts (temporary users and their crontabs) were created for verification and fully cleaned up.
limitations: Command return codes for cmd-20e86bf93bd74c4e (rc=1) and cmd-65a286a7b7e54dab/cmd-15cd9a8dc55a44ab (rc=1) reflect expected negative-test outcomes (missing cron.allow at baseline; a userdel racing against a lingering process) rather than task failures, based on their stdout content.

The captured evidence does not include an explicit final directory listing of /etc/cron.deny content changes beyond the initial empty-file observation, though this does not affect the cron.allow-based restriction since cron.allow takes precedence.

operational_hygiene.summary: State-changing commands were: useradd opsadmin (required), writing /etc/cron.allow (required), creating/removing two disposable test users (crontestdeny, crontestdeny2) with their crontabs to validate enforcement, and the reboot itself (required by the fixed restart-evidence protocol). All test artifacts were cleaned up (cmd-1d70743b914f4bfe removed crontestdeny and its crontab; cmd-65a286a7b7e54dab/cmd-15cd9a8dc55a44ab removed crontestdeny2, requiring a pkill retry after an initial 'user busy' userdel failure, which is a corrective follow-up rather than a new unnecessary mutation). The after_executor temp-file diff shows only an added /tmp/reboot.log (a byproduct of the required backgrounded reboot command) and the expected systemd-private directories tied to the new boot id — no abandoned files, failed services, or unsafe exposure. Listening-socket diff differences are just PID changes from the reboot, not new exposure.
